chapter: Opinions on singers, promotion and originality
title: Bebop speed versus melody and tone
summary: Edison says bebop's speed led white trumpeters to sacrifice quality, and praises Hodges, Webster and Hilton Jefferson for tone.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well, you know, I think the beginning of most of the white soloists' prominence was bebop, was Dizzy. Now, nobody in the world going to be like Dizzy Gillespie. There's only one Dizzy and there will only be one Dizzy. But he took the trumpet and started playing it mostly like a virtuoso, lot of notes. And, you know, that -- a lot of white trumpet players, most of them, they have been taught to play so naturally, they can get over their horn quick, fast, you know.
They can do that.
They can do that. But they can't
hit one note or two notes and make it sound effective and put a lot of feeling in it, you know. And that was the beginning. You don't have to have a lot of quality to play like they play nowadays.
Well, you sacrifice this quality.
Yes. The quality, to get over his horn.
To speed.
Speed, right. And that was the beginning of a lot of white musicians. Charlie Parker.
Charlie Parker could play all those notes, but he could swing.
Oh, yes, he could swing.
More than Dizzy can.

Yeah, but his thing was being able to -- mind working quick and getting over his horn. Speed, you know. Because when it came to using one note on melody, I don't think nobody in the world could play it like Johnny Hodges. He could take a melody and just play it note for note and just absolutely express the most beautiful feelings.
Tell a story.
Oh, yes, you know. And Coleman. And nobody could take the melody and play it as pretty as Ben Webster.
But you see, there's only one. What goes with that speed is really warmth of expression, isn't it.
Yeah, his own. His own, yes. His own
feeling.
I mean, you take Charlie Parker's tone, I mean, it's not a nice tone.
No. There's no quality in it. Not like a Hodges or Benny Carter or Hilton Jefferson, you know. Or -- oh, I could name a lot of them. Like Hilton Jefferson was just absolutely magnificent.
Sure.

A very schooled musician. And he never got the recognition, you know. And then here comes another guy, white, he gets the recognition. And, you know, I just can't -- I just can't laud an imitator. There's no substitute for originality.
That's what Duke said in his book.
You know, there's no substitute.
He said, if two people play exactly the same way, one of them's an imitator.
That's right. One's got to be an imitator, you know. Just like a painting. The original Rembrandt, you know, it's unsellable. Nobody could buy it, it's so precious.
